summary: Integer truncation in Valkey cluster publish message construction causes a heap buffer overflow
description:
## Impact

An authenticated user who can publish to a channel on a server running in
cluster mode can make the server allocate a heap buffer far smaller than
the message it is about to copy into it, and then write past the end of
that buffer with attacker-controlled bytes. This reliably crashes the
server process, and because the overflowing bytes are chosen by the
attacker, it may be possible to escalate it to remote code execution
running as the user the server runs as.

This issue affects Valkey 7.2, 8.0, 8.1, 9.0, 9.1 and 9.2 running in
cluster mode. Servers that do not have cluster mode enabled are not
affected.

## Details

When a node propagates a `PUBLISH` or `SPUBLISH` to the rest of the
cluster, `clusterCreatePublishMsgBlock` in `src/cluster_legacy.c`
(`src/cluster.c` on 7.2) computes the length of the cluster bus message as
a `size_t`, but passes it to `createClusterMsgSendBlock`, which takes a
`uint32_t`. When the channel and message together exceed `UINT32_MAX`, the
length is silently truncated and a buffer far smaller than the message is
allocated. The two `memcpy` calls that follow copy the full channel and
message into it. Both the regular and the light cluster bus header paths
are affected, as are the module publish APIs.

Building a channel and message this large requires more than 4 GiB of
memory. With the default `proto-max-bulk-len` of 512 MB, a client cannot
send arguments that large directly, but a script can construct them on the
server.

The cluster bus cannot represent a message of this size, so the fix
validates the complete serialized length before any 32-bit conversion or
allocation. `PUBLISH` and `SPUBLISH` now reply with an error, and the
message is neither published locally nor propagated.

## Mitigation

You can mitigate this issue by using Valkey ACLs to restrict the scripting
commands (`EVAL`, `EVALSHA`, `EVAL_RO`, `EVALSHA_RO`, `FCALL`, `FCALL_RO`
and `FUNCTION`) if your application does not intend to use them, and by
not raising `proto-max-bulk-len` above its default.

## Credits

The defect was reported by Nenad Stojanovski working with Trend Micro Zero
Day Initiative (ZDI-CAN-28318). The fix was authored by
https://github.com/roshkhatri (#5030).

summary: Use-after-free in the RDMA pending-data handler when a client
description:
## Impact

An authenticated user can run a command that frees another client's
connection while the RDMA transport is processing pending data, leaving a
dangling pointer that is dereferenced shortly after. This reliably crashes
the server process, and the freed heap chunk can be reclaimed with
attacker-influenced bytes.

This issue only affects servers built with RDMA support (`USE_RDMA`) and
configured with an RDMA listener, which is off by default and requires
RDMA-capable hardware. Builds without RDMA are not affected, and the RDMA
transport does not exist before 8.0.

## Details

The RDMA pending-data handler walked its connection list with an iterator
that caches the next entry. Running a client's read handler from inside
that loop can process a command such as `CLIENT KILL`, which synchronously
frees a different client's connection, invalidating the cached entry.
Separately, closing an RDMA connection freed it without removing it from
the pending list, so a stale entry also persisted into later passes.

This is the RDMA equivalent of the TLS issue fixed in GHSA-53mc-f3m3-99vh.

## Mitigation

If you do not need RDMA, build without `USE_RDMA` or do not configure an
RDMA listener. Otherwise, you can mitigate this issue by using Valkey ACLs
to restrict the CLIENT command, in particular `CLIENT KILL`.

## Credits

Reported by Andreas Gabriel Berbescu (aberbescu@gmail.com

summary: Remote DoS with malformed Valkey Cluster bus message
description:
### Impact
A malicious actor with access to the Valkey clusterbus port can send an invalid packet that may cause an out bound read, which might result in the Valkey process being terminated.

### Details
The Valkey clusterbus packet processing code does not validate that a clusterbus ping extension packet is located within the buffer of the clusterbus packet before attempting to read it. Attempting to read memory outside of allocated memory for the process can crash the server.

### Mitigation
We recommend the cluster bus port not be exposed directly to end users and be protected by its own network ACLs.

### Credits
Discovered by 0x Kato <0xkkato@gmail.com>
